claims.text: Adding a minor amount of Ag to CoCrFeNi and then annealing it will induce Ag surface segregation.
The segregated Ag will form a continuous nanoscale Ag-rich surface film.
The Ag-rich film will significantly reduce both coefficient of friction and wear rate from ambient temperature to approximately 600 °C.
Before annealing, the minor Ag addition is present in solid solution within a homogeneous CoCrFeNi-based microstructure.
Annealing at approximately 900 °C in an inert atmosphere for minutes is sufficient to promote Ag migration to the surface.
Annealing temperature, duration, and atmosphere can be optimized to produce a uniform Ag film without harming bulk mechanical properties.
Nanoscale Ag-rich precipitates coalesce into a continuous surface layer.
Ag has a positive enthalpy of mixing with the CoCrFeNi base elements, which drives its segregation to the surface during annealing.
The Ag-rich surface layer has low shear strength.
A low-shear surface film facilitates interfacial shear and reduces direct metal-to-metal contact, thereby lowering friction and wear.
Ag's low melting or softening behavior enhances its lubricity at elevated temperatures and maintains effectiveness over a wide temperature range.
Under matched sliding conditions, the Ag-segregated material will have lower friction and wear than an untreated CoCrFeNi-based HEA.
Untreated CoCrFeNi without Ag segregation typically exhibits higher friction and wear rates.
Keeping the Ag content below 5 at.% will avoid compromising the alloy's bulk properties.
Poorly controlled processing may cause Ag agglomeration, producing discontinuous films and degraded tribological performance.
The long-term stability of the Ag morphology under cyclic high-temperature sliding is uncertain.
